claims.text: Adding Si, Mn, or Al to CrFeCoNi promotes formation and persistence of a stable, coherent, slow-growing oxide layer above 900 °C.
The protective effect of Si, Mn, or Al is mediated by preferential segregation of that element to the metal/oxide interface.
High configurational entropy enables the preferential interfacial segregation of X.
Interfacial segregation of X reduces interfacial-energy and lattice mismatches.
Interfacial segregation of X moderates diffusion and suppresses defects that cause oxide cracking or spallation.
CrFeCoNi alloys lacking an appropriate amount of Si, Mn, or Al fail to develop a protective scale under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneously mixed, single-phase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solution.
High configurational entropy enhances the uniform distribution of X in the alloy.
During high-temperature oxidation, X segregates from the alloy to the surface.
Surface-segregated X reacts to form a slow-growing, stable oxide phase.
The X-containing oxide reduces local strain and interfacial energy, thereby minimizing cracks and spallation.
An optimal X content will produce a more continuous, coherent, and slowly growing protective oxide than either no X or a non-optimal X concentration.
CrFeCoNi without Si, Mn, or Al is the control baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive high-temperature service atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism is limited to X concentrations sufficient to cause segregation without compromising the single-phase structure.
Oxide thickness, growth rate, continuity, adherence, phase composition, cracking, and spallation can be compared after matched high-temperature exposures.
The hypothesis is falsified if an X-containing alloy exhibits cracking or spallation rates similar to or greater than the CrFeCoNi baseline under matched conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if the CrFeCoNi baseline forms an oxide scale with growth rate and coherence comparable to the X-containing alloy.
